title: Parse Lisp Expression
constraints: expression has no leading or trailing spaces
Tokens in expression are separated by exactly one space
The answer and every intermediate value fit in a signed 32-bit integer
expression is valid and evaluates to an integer

examples.name: Example 1
input: (let x 2 (mult x (let x 3 y 4 (add x y))))

examples.name: Example 3
input: (let x 1 y 2 x (add x y) (add x y))

tests.name: Test 4
input: (let x -2 y x (let y 3 (mult x y)))

tests.name: Test 7
input: (let x 1 (let y x (let x (add y 1) (mult x (add x y)))))

tests.name: Test 8
input: (let foo (mult 4 5) bar (add foo foo) (let foo 1 (add foo bar)))

tests.name: Test 11
input: (let x (let x 5 y 6 (mult x y)) y (add x -100) z (let x 9 x) (add (add x y) z))

notes:
## Intuition

The language is a tree: every parenthesised form contains smaller expressions. A recursive parser that reads one token at a time mirrors that tree exactly, and evaluates each form the moment its parts are known. The only subtle rule is scope, and a stack of maps models it directly: entering a `let` pushes a fresh map, leaving it pops the map, and a name is looked up from the top of the stack down. A simpler but slower route re-splits substrings at every level and copies the whole environment for each `let`.

## Approach

1. Put a space on the inner side of every parenthesis and split on spaces, so `tokens` holds `(`, `)`, names, numbers and keywords.
2. `parse()` consumes one expression starting at `pos` and returns its value.
3. A token other than `(` is an atom: a name (starts with a letter) is resolved by `lookup`, anything else is a number.
4. After `(` read `op`. For `add` and `mult` parse two expressions and combine them.
5. For `let`, push a new map. While the next token is a name that is not the last part of the form, bind it to the value of the expression after it. Then parse the final expression and pop the map.
6. Skip the closing `)` and return the value.

## Example 1, step by step

`(let x 2 (mult x (let x 3 y 4 (add x y))))`: the outer `let` pushes a map and binds `x = 2`. Its body is a `mult`: the first operand `x` is found in that map, giving `2`. The second operand is a `let` that pushes a second map with `x = 3` and `y = 4`; inside it `(add x y)` finds `x = 3` in the top map first, so it is `7`. That map is popped, and `mult` returns `2 * 7 = 14`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n · d): each token is read once, and a lookup walks at most `d` nested scopes.
- Space: O(n) for the tokens, the scope maps and the recursion.

## Pitfalls

- A `let` part that is followed by `)` is the result expression, even when it is a plain name or number.
- Bind pairs one at a time so a later pair sees earlier ones, including a rebound name.
- Pop the scope when the `let` ends, otherwise inner bindings leak into the enclosing form.
- Numbers can start with `-`; test the first character for a letter rather than for a digit.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `tokens` | the expression split into parentheses, keywords, names and numbers |
| `pos` | index of the next unread token |
| `scopes` | stack of maps, one per open `let`, from name to value |
| `token`, `op` | the token just read and the form's keyword |
| `first`, `value` | the left operand and the value of the current form |
| `name` | the variable a `let` pair is binding |

narration.2: Pad every parenthesis with a space and split, so each parenthesis, keyword, name and number becomes its own token.
narration.3: The scope stack starts empty; each open let will push one map of its bindings.
narration.4: pos is the index of the next token the parser has not consumed yet.
narration.7: Search the scopes from the innermost one outward.
narration.9: The first scope that knows the name holds the binding in effect, so return its value.
narration.15: Read the first token of the expression that starts at pos.
narration.16: Anything other than an opening parenthesis is a single-token atom.
narration.17: A token starting with a letter is a variable to look up; otherwise it is an integer, possibly negative.
narration.19: After the opening parenthesis comes the keyword: add, mult or let.
narration.22: Evaluate the first operand; the recursive call advances pos past it.
narration.23: Evaluate the second operand and add the two.
narration.26: Same pattern for mult, multiplying the two operands.
narration.28: A let opens a new scope, so push an empty map for its bindings.
narration.29: Keep binding while the next token is a name that is not the last part of the form.
narration.30: Take the variable name of this pair.
narration.31: Evaluate its expression with the bindings made so far and store it in the innermost scope.
narration.33: What remains is the final expression; its value is the value of the whole let.
narration.34: Close the scope so these bindings stop hiding outer ones.
narration.36: Step over the closing parenthesis of this form.
narration.40: Parse the one expression that makes up the whole input and return its value.
